stories.headline: Magyar demands President Sulyok resign; photo-exclusion incident triggers national debate
stories.summary: PM Magyar repeatedly called on Fidesz-appointed President Tamás Sulyok to resign during and after the swearing-in ceremony, and instructed new ministers to exclude Sulyok from official group photographs at the Sándor Palace appointment ceremony on May 12. The MTI state news agency was found to have cropped Sulyok from published photos, triggering an internal investigation by the state media regulator. Polls showed 60% of Hungarians support Sulyok resigning, but Sulyok refuses and constitutional lawyers debated removal procedures. Fidesz accused Magyar of humiliating the presidency and attempting unconstitutional pressure on independent institutions.

stories.headline: Magyar's Tisza government formally takes office, ending sixteen years of Orbán rule
stories.summary: Péter Magyar was sworn in as PM on May 9 and his 16-minister Tisza cabinet was formally appointed by President Sulyok on May 12, marking the first non-Orbán government since 2010. The inauguration featured symbolic gestures including the EU flag returned to parliament, Roma children performing the Roma anthem, and Magyar immediately calling on Sulyok to resign. International coverage was extensive, with the Guardian editorial and Reuters framing it as a democratic-renewal test case for Europe.

stories.headline: Magyar fires Orbán's former press chief Havasi; legal dispute over dismissal's validity erupts
stories.summary: PM Magyar dismissed Bertalan Havasi — Viktor Orbán's longtime press secretary who remained as deputy state secretary in the Cabinet Office — via a Saturday-evening government gazette notice. Havasi responded with a combative public letter demanding his six-month severance, calling Magyar 'Öcsi' (little brother). Fidesz politicians Gulyás Gergely and Rétvári Bence challenged the legality of the firing, claiming it referenced a minister position that no longer exists; a fact-check by Telex confirmed the dismissal was legally valid. Magyar also announced Orbán himself would not receive his 38.8 million forint severance under existing rules.

stories.headline: Magyar opens Karmelita and government buildings to public, removes iconic security fencing
stories.summary: PM Magyar personally dismantled security barriers around the Karmelita Monastery — Orbán's former office — on May 15-16 and led press tours through the building and the former Rogán-led Cabinet Office, framing the gesture as a break with Orbán-era secrecy and opulence. The buildings were opened to public visits. Le Monde and AP covered the tours internationally; domestic media accompanied Magyar through both buildings.

stories.summary: PM Magyar released photos of the Kúria's (Supreme Court) renovation — claiming it features a bar, gilded ceilings, and a presidential suite — and called for Chief Justice Varga Zs. András to resign. The Kúria denied the characterizations in a press release, and the Hungarian Judges' Association responded with photos of underfunded ordinary courts. Fidesz accused Magyar of unconstitutionally attempting to subordinate the independent judiciary.

stories.headline: Orbán gives first interviews as opposition leader; forint and fiscal data dominate his messaging
stories.summary: In his first major interview since losing office (published Saturday in Magyar Nemzet), former PM Orbán described his 16 years as Hungary's most successful era, denied corruption allegations, and vowed Fidesz would rebuild as a 'tiger.' He also addressed the Balásy advertising scandal, the loss of young voters, and pledged to protect Fidesz voters from political retaliation. Magyar responded sharply, calling Orbán's framing 'nonsense.'

stories.headline: Orbán severance pay blocked; former ministers' payouts redirected to Ukrainian orphanage
stories.summary: Magyar announced former ministers and Orbán himself would not receive their legally mandated severance payments. Orbán pre-empted this by announcing he would donate his 38.8 million forint entitlement to a Hungarian children's home in Transcarpathia, Ukraine. Magyar accepted and asked Orbán to also persuade Havasi Bertalan to forgo his payout. Multiple domestic and international outlets covered the dispute, which also touched on whether Magyar's government could legally block the payouts.

stories.headline: MNB executes implicit rate cut, forint weakens after post-election rally; credit agencies review Hungary
stories.summary: The Hungarian National Bank under governor Varga Mihály conducted an implicit rate cut via an FX-swap facility adjustment, signaling that the post-election forint surge had become too strong for Hungarian exporters. The forint had strengthened dramatically after the Tisza election win but retreated after the MNB action. Analysts at MBH Bank forecast a formal rate-cut cycle starting June. Separately, S&P and Fitch were both scheduled to review Hungary's sovereign rating, with Fitch noting the economy has stagnated since 2023. The MNB also awarded the Lámfalussy Prize to the Polish central bank governor at its annual conference.

stories.headline: Hungary summons Russian ambassador over massive Ukraine drone attack near its border
stories.summary: PM Magyar's new government summoned Russian ambassador Evgeny Stanislavov for consultations after Russia launched one of its largest drone attacks, which came close to Hungary's border with Ukraine in Transcarpathia. Foreign Minister Anita Orbán met with the ambassador to ask when Putin 'plans to finally end this bloody war.' President Sulyok also condemned the attack. The move marked a significant rhetorical shift from Orbán-era deference toward Moscow.

stories.headline: Hungary races to unlock €10.4 billion in frozen EU funds before August deadline; lifts Israel veto
stories.summary: EU officials said Hungary could still meet the August 31 deadline to qualify for €10.4 billion in frozen pandemic recovery funds if it enacts required rule-of-law reforms quickly. On the day Magyar took office, Hungary lifted the veto that had blocked new EU sanctions against Israeli settlers; the EU approved its first new Israel-related sanctions package as a result. The Guardian and Washington Post both tied the EU funds opportunity to Magyar's reform agenda.
